posts.title: Sepulveda Subway: Fashion Square Is on Metro's Yard Shortlist
posts.description: Metro is studying Westfield Fashion Square as one of five rail yard sites for the Sepulveda subway. Here are the Sherman Oaks scoping meeting dates and the November 18 comment deadline.
posts.body:
Westfield Fashion Square sits on Riverside Drive. Bloomingdale's and Macy's anchor it, and a newer row of outward-facing tenants includes Kura Revolving Sushi Bar, Panini Kabob Grill and the BoxUnion boxing studio. Its owner, Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield, lists 144 shops and 3,863 parking spaces at the center, which it has owned since 2002.

It is also the first entry on a short list LA Metro published for the Sepulveda Transit Corridor. That list names five places where the subway's trains could be stored and maintained. "Option 1" reads, in full, "At the existing Westfield Fashion Sq on Riverside Dr." Metro is taking public comment on that list, and on station locations, through November 18. Two of its five scoping meetings are in the Valley, and one is on Van Nuys Boulevard in Sherman Oaks.

### The Argument Sherman Oaks Already Won

For several years the local debate centered on Sepulveda Boulevard and the risk of elevated trains running above it. The [Sherman Oaks Neighborhood Council](https://www.shermanoaksnc.org/page/viewNews/7904) voted 11–0 on July 8, 2024, to support dropping Alternative 4. It had already backed fully underground heavy rail and opposed elevated trains on Sepulveda.

That question has been settled. On January 22, 2026, the Metro Board unanimously selected Modified Alternative 5, an underground, automated heavy-rail subway that runs beneath Van Nuys Boulevard in the Valley. Metro's own summary of what the community asked for includes "No aerial alignment along Sepulveda Bl in the San Fernando Valley" and "No ventilation shaft in the Santa Monica Mountains."

The Sherman Oaks stop moved along with the route. The earlier Alternative 5 placed its Valley station at Ventura and Sepulveda. The selected plan puts it at Ventura and Van Nuys. The full line would cover about 12.3 miles with seven underground stations, from the Van Nuys Metrolink station down to the E Line at Expo/Sepulveda. Trains would run in a single-bore tunnel every 2.5 minutes at peak. According to [Metro's FAQ](https://cloud.sfmc.metro.net/STC_FAQ_English), the tunnel between the Ventura station and UCLA would run "more than 1.5 miles east of the 405."

Support came from many directions. [Streetsblog LA](https://la.streetsblog.org/2026/01/14/metro-committee-approves-sepulveda-rail-alignment-postpones-torrance-rail-approval) listed the neighborhood council among the groups backing the plan at the January committee hearing. The Sherman Oaks Homeowners Association board voted unanimously in favor. In [her statement](https://lindseyhorvath.lacounty.gov/lpa-sepulveda-transit/), Supervisor Lindsey Horvath called it a generational investment. The Los Angeles City Council adopted a [resolution from Councilmember Nithya Raman](https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-0046_misc_1-14-26.pdf) supporting the choice on February 17, 2026, by a 14–0–1 vote.

### Why Metro Is Asking the Neighborhood Again

The plan everyone supported was one Metro had not fully studied. The 2025 Draft Environmental Impact Report analyzed five alternatives. Modified Alternative 5 was a sixth, combining Alternative 5's subway technology with Alternative 6's route under Van Nuys Boulevard. Bob Anderson, transportation chair of the Sherman Oaks Homeowners Association, writes in [the association's transit updates](https://www.shermanoakshomeownersassociation.com/what-we-do/transit) that Metro announced at an April 2026 meeting that it would need to recirculate the environmental report to cover the new hybrid.

That process has now started. According to [Metro's project page](https://www.metro.net/projects/sepulvedacorridor/), the Federal Transit Administration and Metro are holding a scoping period ahead of a federal environmental document under the National Environmental Policy Act and a Recirculated Draft EIR under the California Environmental Quality Act. Metro is asking for comments on "the project's purpose and need; project elements, including station and maintenance/storage facility locations; and potential environmental impacts."

Choosing the mode was the citywide decision. Station locations and the maintenance yard are where the plan meets specific blocks, and that part is open for comment now.

### Five Yard Sites, One on Riverside Drive

A heavy-rail line needs a maintenance and storage facility, a yard where trains are parked, cleaned and repaired. Metro says these candidate sites were chosen to allow building the line in phases and to give options for environmental analysis and community input.

| Option | Location as Metro describes it |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | At the existing Westfield Fashion Sq on Riverside Dr |
| 2 | Along Oxnard St between Kester Av and Sepulveda Bl |
| 3 | On existing Metro parking and adjacent properties near the G Line Van Nuys Station |
| 4 | North of Victory Bl, immediately west of Van Nuys Bl |
| 5 | At The Plant shopping center and adjacent properties east of Van Nuys Bl |

Phasing explains why five sites are listed. The Board also chose an Initial Operating Segment of about 8.4 miles between the Wilshire/Westwood station and the G Line/Van Nuys station, which would be built first. Metro describes two ways to handle the yard in phases. A smaller first yard could be expanded later for the full line, or a smaller yard could be paired with a second site built later. Options 3 and 4 fall into the second category, because both would also need Option 5 at The Plant once the full line is built.

The Fashion Square option is new. The 2025 Draft EIR placed heavy-rail yards for the earlier alternatives west of Woodman Avenue and south of the Metrolink Ventura County Line tracks, and it did not name the mall. During that round, LADWP objected to sites east of the Van Nuys Metrolink station because of conflicts with its operations and the planned Mid-Valley Water Facility. The regional rail authority, SCRRA, raised possible interference with its own operations and future expansion. In January the Board directed staff to develop a "refined maintenance and storage strategy." The current list came out of that work.

Every site on the list is a candidate for study, and Metro has not picked one. Its published description says the facility would be "at" the existing mall. It gives no acreage, parcel boundary or footprint, and it does not say whether a yard would take all of the property or part of it. Meanwhile the mall itself has been adding tenants. In the SOHA newsletter in June 2026, association president Matt Epstein wrote that he found Fashion Square busy on a late afternoon. He noted BoxUnion's arrival and said Noodle St appeared close to opening.

### What the Recirculated Report Still Has to Show

Several details that matter most for a block-by-block view of Sherman Oaks have not been published yet.

- The route under homes. Metro says exact information on which properties the route will pass under "will be included in the Recirculated Draft EIR."

- The Ventura/Van Nuys station layout. Current materials give no entrance count, entrance locations or station footprint.

- Construction at street level. Metro's FAQ says bored-tunnel construction "generally produce[s] no noticeable noise, vibration, or settlement at the ground surface." It names stations, tunnel boring machine launch and retrieval sites, and points where the tunnel meets the surface as the places where construction would be noticeable. Staging areas and construction methods for the Ventura station have not been identified.

- Cost. Metro's January announcement put a preliminary $24.2 billion estimate, in 2023 dollars, on the original Alternative 5, to be updated as the modified design develops. Measure M's spending plan sets aside $5.7 billion in 2015 dollars. Metro is still considering a public-private partnership to cover the rest.

The Sherman Oaks Homeowners Association has also asked about noise and vibration beneath Sherman Oaks and Bel Air. It has questioned the phased plan, which would open two Valley stations first, at Ventura Boulevard and the G Line at Oxnard Street, and leave the Metrolink connection for later.

### The Calendar, Near and Far

The near-term dates are fixed. According to [Metro's project page](https://www.metro.net/projects/sepulvedacorridor/), the scoping meetings are:

- Wednesday, November 4, noon to 1 p.m., on Zoom

- Saturday, November 7, 3 to 5 p.m., Culver City Veterans Memorial Building, 4117 Overland Avenue

- Tuesday, November 10, 5:30 to 7:30 p.m., Westwood United Methodist Church, 10497 Wilshire Boulevard

- Saturday, November 14, 10 a.m. to noon, Marvin Braude Constituent Center, 6262 Van Nuys Boulevard

- Monday, November 16, 5:30 to 7:30 p.m., Sherman Oaks East Valley Adult Center, 5056 Van Nuys Boulevard, Building B

Spanish interpretation will be available at every meeting. Other accommodations can be requested by calling 213.922.7375 at least 72 hours ahead. Comments can also be submitted through [Metro's online comment form](https://metro.commentinput.com/?id=7aD5AtTpF), by email to sepulvedatransit@metro.net, by phone at the same number, or by mail to project manager Peter Carter at One Gateway Plaza. All comments are due November 18, 2026.

The longer timeline is less clear. Metro's FAQ says the project is still in planning and that an updated construction timeline will be shared when available. The project is not on [Metro's 28x28 list](https://www.metro.net/28x28/) of projects meant to be ready for the 2028 Games. In its October 2026 update, SOHA said California Public Records Act requests it filed in September showed design work running to March 2027 and environmental work to the end of 2028. The association also published an AI-generated estimate of more than $80 billion and an opening "well into the 2040s." Those figures are SOHA's own advocacy estimate, not Metro numbers.

So the first chance Sherman Oaks has to shape where the yard and the Ventura/Van Nuys station go is the four weeks before November 18. The Recirculated Draft EIR will then answer these questions in detail, including which properties sit above the tunnel.

If you own near Van Nuys Boulevard, Riverside Drive or the blocks south of Ventura and want to talk through what this process could mean for your plans, Stacey Leahy is glad to go over the published maps with you before the November 16 meeting. Let's Connect.

posts.title: Burbank Airport's New Terminal: What Changed for Local Drivers
posts.description: Same 14 gates and runways, but a new entrance off Winona, no waiting at the curb, Lot E closed, and new garage rates. A Burbank resident's guide to the new BUR terminal.
posts.body:
"Instead of turning right, you turn left." That was how Southwest pilot Mike Petros described his taxi to the new gate on opening morning, as reported by the [Los Angeles Times](https://www.latimes.com/travel/story/2026-10-13/burbank-airport-new-terminal-opening-day). His line also fits anyone driving to the airport from Burbank, Toluca Lake or Studio City this fall.

Hollywood Burbank Airport's $1.3 billion replacement terminal opened at 5 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, and first flights were scheduled for 7 a.m. Every arrival and departure now runs through the new building. It took 33 months to build, and it sits on the opposite side of the airfield from the old terminals. Nine days in, most of what changed for a local traveler is how you get to the building, where the car goes and how pickups work. The flight itself is close to what it always was.

### Fourteen Gates and a New Front Door

The terminal replaced the old one without making the airport bigger. The Los Angeles Times reported the same two runways and the same 14 gates. On opening day the schedule called for about 90 arrivals and departures across eight airlines, roughly the same as in the old buildings. Passengers still often board from the front and back of the plane, on outdoor stairs from the tarmac.

That leaves the changes concentrated in a fairly small part of the trip.

| | Before October 13 | Since October 13 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main entrance | Off Thornton Avenue | Winona Avenue and Hollywood Way |
| Lot E | Open | Permanently closed |
| Valet | Old terminal valet center | Valet Center in the Terminal Garage |
| Baggage claim | Outdoor carousels | Indoor, three carousels |
| TSA screening lanes | Five | Eight |
| Gates | 14 | 14 |
| Total parking spaces | 6,637 | 6,637 |

If you've used BUR for years, the change most likely to catch you is the first row. According to the [Daily News](https://www.dailynews.com/2026/10/13/hollywood-burbank-airport-celebrates-new-terminal-completing-1-3-billion-project), the main entrance moved from its longtime spot off Thornton Avenue to Winona Avenue and Hollywood Way. The Times reported that the airport sent staff to redirect travelers who went to the idle old terminals first, and that one passenger heard about the switch from his Uber driver on the way in.

### The Curb Has Rules Now

With the entrance moved, the next thing to relearn is the pickup. The airport's [FAQ](https://hollywoodburbankairport.com/pages/faq) says you can drop off or pick up at the terminal curb, but you can't wait there. If your passenger isn't already at the curb when you pull up, the airport asks you to park in the Short Term structure. The same page says to wait for arriving passengers in baggage claim, with the car in that structure and posted rates in effect. The FAQ doesn't point to any separate free waiting area.

So the price of arriving early is easy to work out. These are the rates on the airport's [parking pages](https://hollywoodburbankairport.com/pages/parking) as of publication:

- Terminal Garage: $9 for the first hour, $5 for each additional 30 minutes, $49 daily maximum.

- Lot F: $5 for the first hour, $3 for each additional 30 minutes, $28 daily maximum, with shuttle service.

- Lot G: $5 for the first hour, $3 for each additional 30 minutes, $24 daily maximum, with shuttle service.

- Valet: at the Valet Center in the Terminal Garage, $59 daily maximum.

The airport says posted prices include the City of Burbank parking tax, that its lots are open 24/7 and that the maximum stay is 30 days. By those numbers, picking someone up after waiting 90 minutes costs $14 in the Terminal Garage. For a weeklong trip, Lot G's daily cap is less than half the garage's.

The new garage has about 2,000 spaces and 310 EV charging ports. The airport's total stays at 6,637 spaces, the same as before. Rideshare pickup is now at the ground-transportation island in front of the parking structure's main entrance. Rental cars are still at the Regional Intermodal Transportation Center across Hollywood Way, and customers take a shuttle there.

### Inside, the Gains Are Measured in Feet and Lanes

Once you're through the doors, the new building does make the airport feel different. It covers about 355,000 square feet, compared with 232,000 for the complex it replaced. The extra space mostly went to the parts of the trip where people tend to queue.

Security has eight TSA lanes, up from five. Airport officials say the walk from the entrance to the farthest gate is now 1,285 feet, down from 1,600. Corridors are wider, and every seat has access to power, mostly USB-C. Baggage claim has moved indoors. The airport's indoor claim area has three carousels.

The building also comes with art. The Times described mirrored grid artwork by Glenn Kaino hanging overhead and two illuminated steel sculptures by Cliff Garten on either side of the main entrance, along with terrazzo floors and landscaping planted with cactus and succulents.

[LAist](https://laist.com/brief/news/transportation/hollywood-burbank-airport-terminal-open) reported a mostly smooth first day, with some last-minute gate changes and some flight-information screens showing the wrong information.

### The Restaurants Are Still Catching Up

On opening day the dining was the clearest gap. The Los Angeles Times reported that most of the six retail stores were open but none of the 13 food concessions was fully operating. Two were offering grab-and-go, and an airport spokesperson said more options would open later that day and that week.

The airport's [restaurants and shopping directory](https://www.hollywoodburbankairport.com/pages/restaurants-shopping) lists the full lineup. It includes Perry's Joint, Farm Table Bistro, Jones Coffee, Guy Fieri's Flavortown, Spring Kitchen, Poquito Mas, a smash-burger counter, Pete's Pub, Diane's Italian Market, Massis Kabob, Starbucks, Border Grill and Jet Tila's. The directory doesn't say which ones are serving yet. If your flight is early or you're traveling with children, it's worth bringing something to eat until the counters you want are open. The Times describes Pete's Pub as having picture-window views of the runways and the Verdugo Mountains, which may make it the place to wait out a delay once the full menu is running.

### The Train Connection Shifted Too

Moving the terminal also changed the trip for Metrolink riders. Metrolink's [BUR airport shuttle page](https://metrolinktrains.com/rider-info/general-info/airports/hollywood-burbank-bur-airport-shuttle), with directions that apply from October 13, says the Antelope Valley Line's North Station connects to the new terminal by a walk of about half a mile via Cohasset Street, or by a free on-demand shuttle. Riders on the Ventura County Line use South Station and connect through the RITC on a free airport shuttle.

The airport's own buses-and-trains page still describes shuttle pickup at the Lot C shuttle island and the valet area. Metrolink's page is the one written for the new layout, so follow its directions until the two match.

### What Happens to the Old Terminal and Lot E

A few things on the old side of the airfield still need tidying up. The Daily News reported that Lot E is closing permanently with the move. The airport gives anyone whose car was still in the old terminal garage or valet center 30 days from that date to collect it. Counting from October 13, that deadline falls around November 12. If you, a neighbor or a houseguest parked there before a long trip, now is a good time to check.

The old terminals are now empty. Their original buildings, in a Spanish Colonial Revival style, date to 1930. [KTLA](https://www.ktla.com/news/local-news/hollywood-burbank-airport-new-terminal-opens) reported that airport officials expect to demolish them within the next 12 months. The Daily News traced the project back to Measure B, which Burbank voters approved in 2016 to let the Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority build the replacement.

For the next trip, the practical version is short. Turn in at Winona Avenue and Hollywood Way. Don't count on waiting at the curb. Pick your lot by how long you'll be away, and for now, plan to bring a snack.

How easy it is to get to the airport is one of those everyday details that shapes how a neighborhood feels to live in, and it's the kind of thing Stacey Leahy watches closely across Burbank and the nearby Valley communities. If you'd like a calm, well-informed conversation about what changes like this mean for your own plans, let's connect.

posts.title: Valencia Mello-Roos: Billed by Square Foot, Up 2% Each July
posts.description: In Valencia's newer districts, the Mello-Roos tax depends on a home's floor area and rises 2% every July. Here is how two homes at one price end up with different tax bills.
posts.body:
In the newest part of Valencia, the Mello-Roos tax has nothing to do with what you pay for the house. It depends on the floor area recorded on the original building permit. Picture two homes in the same district at the same price. The one with more square feet falls into a higher tax class, and that class goes up by 2% every July 1 for decades.

A Santa Clarita Valley buyer has usually checked the median price already. According to Southland Regional Association of Realtors figures released September 9, 2026, the single-family median was $865,000 in August 2026, down 2.8% from a year earlier. A median compares homes by price. The special tax compares them by size and by the date their district was formed. For that reason, the home that looks like the best value per square foot can come with the largest tax.

### The Tax Table Counts Square Feet

Los Angeles County's CFD No. 2021-01, called Valencia-Facilities, covers the western Santa Clarita Valley west of Interstate 5 and south of State Route 126. Its improvement areas have been added in phases. The Board of Supervisors approved Improvement Area No. 3 on October 17, 2023. The [rate and method of apportionment](https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/184930.pdf) in that packet places each detached home in a tax class based on its residential floor area. Floor area is taken from the original building permit, and the CFD Administrator can consider later permit documents to allocate the tax fairly.

The table below shows the county's starting rates for fiscal year 2023-24. The FY 2026-27 column is our estimate. It applies the three 2% increases the document schedules for July 1 of 2024, 2025, and 2026. It is not a quote from any parcel's tax bill.

| Detached home floor area | FY 2023-24 assigned tax | FY 2026-27, estimated at 2% per year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 2,601 sq ft | $3,017 | about $3,202 |
| 2,601 to 2,800 sq ft | $3,847 | about $4,083 |
| 2,801 to 3,000 sq ft | $4,263 | about $4,524 |
| 3,001 to 3,200 sq ft | $4,679 | about $4,965 |
| 3,401 to 3,600 sq ft | $5,509 | about $5,846 |
| 3,801 to 4,000 sq ft | $6,340 | about $6,728 |
| 4,201 sq ft or larger | $7,172 | about $7,611 |

The difference between the smallest and largest detached classes is about $4,400 a year in the current fiscal year, or roughly $367 a month. That money buys no extra land or features. It is the cost of the larger square-foot class.

### Every July Adds 2%, and the Record Shows It

The county document requires the assigned rates to rise by 2% of the prior year's amount every July 1, beginning July 1, 2024. The tax ends when the bonds reach final maturity or 40 years after the levy begins, whichever comes first. It cannot be levied after fiscal year 2063-64. A 2% annual increase compounds to about double over 35 years. A household buying into the smallest class today could be paying roughly what the largest class pays now well before the levy ends.

For a district that has been running longer, the William S. Hart Union High School District's CFD No. 2015-1 shows what the escalator does over time. It covers an area south of Plum Canyon Road, north of Newhall Ranch Road, and east and west of Golden Valley Road. The district formed it in 2015 and authorized up to $35 million in bonded debt. Its [annual special tax report](https://4.files.edl.io/0777/08/10/21/152707-3337e36b-3b40-4bbf-8a55-8d1f2a69a9c8.pdf) lists the original rates with the same 2% clause, starting July 1, 2017.

- Under 1,900 sq ft: $2,037.17 in FY 2016-17, then $2,249.20 in FY 2021-22

- Over 4,099 sq ft: $4,038.29 in FY 2016-17, then $4,458.58 in FY 2021-22

The same report shows how homes in that district were distributed across the classes in FY 2021-22. There were 39 homes in the smallest class and 22 in the largest, out of 494 developed units. The total levy came to $1,556,940.82. So the class system is not a rare edge case. It sets the bill for every home in the tract.

### How One Price Splits Into Two Costs

Imagine two detached homes in Improvement Area No. 3, both priced near the August 2026 valley median. One has about 2,500 square feet. The other has about 4,300 square feet, perhaps because it is older inside or sits on a less favored lot. On a price-per-square-foot basis, the larger home looks like the better buy. Under the county's table, though, it falls in the top class. The smaller home falls in the bottom one.

Using the estimated FY 2026-27 rates, the larger home's special tax runs about $4,400 a year more. Both bills grow 2% each July, so the dollar gap between them grows too. Ordinary property tax depends on the purchase price, so it would be about the same for both homes. The only thing that differs is the CFD line, and it differs because of the square-foot class.

A listing price can't show this. The median can't either. Both measure what the market will pay. The CFD measures something else, and it was fixed years before the current owner bought.

### The Smaller Line Items Follow the Same Logic

Santa Clarita also has its own [Landscape Maintenance Districts](https://santaclarita.gov/specialdistricts/landscape-maintenance-districts). The city manages 62 financially independent zones. Each zone's revenue can be spent only in its own benefit area, and the first zones were created in Valencia's Old Orchard area. LMD charges are special assessments. They are separate from Mello-Roos and from any private HOA fee. One parcel can sit inside several districts at once, and the charges add together.

The city's [FY 2025-26 engineer's report](https://santaclarita.gov/specialdistricts/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2025/08/FY2526-Consolidated-LLD_Final1.pdf) lists applied residential rates by zone:

- Skyline Ranch, zone T-2A: $104.52 per EBU

- West Creek, zone T-68: $153.51 per EBU

- Fair Oaks Ranch, zone T-65A: $200 per EBU, listed in the city's zone directory as Ranch at Fair Oaks

- Tesoro del Valle, zone T-76: $103.83 per parcel

Streetlight assessments for FY 2025-26 were $12.38 per EBU in Zone A and $66 per EBU in Zone B. Zone B's maximum is tied to CPI. The same report applies a 3.42% CPI increase to the applicable maximum rates and exempts certain zones from that adjustment. The city's FAQ says assessments are apportioned by benefit and cannot go above an established maximum unless property owners approve.

These amounts are a fraction of a Valencia-Facilities bill. They work the same way, though. The parcel's location sets the charge, and an adjustment mechanism moves it over time. To find a home's total, you add up every district its parcel sits in.

The city also has its own [community facilities districts](https://santaclarita.gov/finance/community-facilities-districts), separate from the county and school district ones. They include Valencia Town Center No. 2002-1, Vista Canyon No. 2016-1, and Cooper Street Parking Structure No. 2020-1. The city notes that Valencia Town Center's 2002 bonds were refinanced in 2012 and paid for public infrastructure.

### Where the Line Reads Zero

Not every new Santa Clarita community carries a CFD. The Daily News [reported in March 2026](https://www.dailynews.com/2026/03/18/new-santa-clarita-homes-from-800ks-with-no-mello-roos/) that Pelona Hills at Sand Canyon, a 119-home community from Intracorp Homes, launched with prices starting in the low $800,000s and is not subject to Mello-Roos. Its homes range from 1,830 to 2,181 square feet. The site is on the east side of the valley near State Route 14 and the Vista Canyon Metrolink station.

That price range overlaps the valley's single-family median. As a result, a buyer looking at both sides of the valley at the same budget may be comparing a home with no Mello-Roos line against one with a CFD bill of several thousand dollars a year that rises every July. The difference in monthly cost comes from district boundaries and formation dates, not from the homes themselves.

### Reading a Parcel Before an Offer

The Southland Regional Association of Realtors puts it directly in its [Santa Clarita Valley area disclosure](https://srar.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SCV-AREA-Disclosure-May-11-2026.pdf), updated May 11, 2026:

"Buyer should be aware they may be subject to change in amounts and duration and Buyer should not rely on these types of taxes or bonds ending and should check with appropriate entities and administrators regarding these taxes and bonds as to amounts and duration."

The same disclosure explains where the figures appear during a transaction. It also says LMD assessments and services can change, and that some maintenance may shift to individual homeowners. Each of these sources answers a different question:

- The Natural Hazard Disclosure report delivered in escrow. The association notes it lists Mello-Roos, bonds, and taxes, along with contact information for the administrator.

- The parcel's current tax bill. It shows each district charge billed this year, including any LMD or streetlight assessments.

- The CFD administrator. The administrator can confirm the tax class, the escalation schedule, and the final levy year for that parcel.

A buyer comparing homes can line up the size class, the district, and the escalator side by side, the same way they would compare kitchens. These details are on record before an offer is written. They are in the public documents, but they are hard to find there.

### A Few Questions Buyers Ask

Does the Mello-Roos amount depend on what I pay for the home?
In Valencia-Facilities Improvement Area No. 3 and in Hart CFD No. 2015-1, the assigned tax depends on floor-area class, not purchase price.

Will the tax end after a set number of years?
In Improvement Area No. 3, it ends at final bond maturity or 40 years after the levy begins, whichever comes first, and no later than FY 2063-64. Other districts have their own terms. The SRAR disclosure advises buyers not to assume a tax ends.

Is an LMD assessment the same as an HOA fee?
No. The city treats LMD charges as public special assessments. They are separate from private HOA dues and from Mello-Roos.

If you're weighing homes across the Santa Clarita Valley and want to see each parcel's district charges laid out before you decide, Stacey Leahy can review the tax class, escalator, and assessment zones on every home on your list with you, so you're comparing costs and not just prices. Let's Connect.

This article is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. Consult a qualified professional about your situation.

posts.title: Westside Transfer Tax Cliffs: ULA vs. Santa Monica's GS
posts.description: In Brentwood and the Palisades, a home sale's tax jumps at $5.4M. In Santa Monica, the jump comes at $8M. Here's how each threshold changes asking prices, listings and remodel decisions in 2026.
posts.body:
A Brentwood homeowner planned to sell and then worked through the closing costs. The City of Los Angeles transfer tax plus agent commissions would have taken about 11% of the sale proceeds, so the owners kept the house and put that money into rebuilding it. Their builder, Oren Levy of Gesh Group, described the decision to The Real Deal in July 2026.

That house never reached the market. Across much of the Westside, this is the main effect of the city's "mansion tax." Price cuts have mattered less than a quiet loss of homes that would have sold above a certain price and were never listed. Where that price sits depends on which city the lot is in.

### A Tax on the Whole Price, Not the Overage

Measure ULA applies inside City of Los Angeles limits, which is why Brentwood and Pacific Palisades sales show up in the city's ULA revenue data. For sales closing after June 30, 2026, the Office of Finance applies a 4% ULA tax to sales above $5,400,000 and 5.5% to sales of $10,900,000 or more. Both sit on top of the city's 0.45% base transfer tax. The rate applies to the full sale price, not just the amount over the threshold. So a sale that crosses $5.4 million picks up roughly $216,000 in ULA tax all at once. Crossing $10.9 million adds about $163,500 more.

Santa Monica is a separate city, so ULA doesn't apply there. The [City of Santa Monica](https://santamonica.gov/documentary-transfer-tax-real-property-transfer-tax) 's Measure GS schedule charges $3 per $1,000 below $5 million, $6 per $1,000 from $5 million to just under $8 million, and $56 per $1,000 at $8 million or more. The city's own example puts an $8 million transfer at $448,000 in city tax plus $8,800 in county tax.

Here is what that means at the same sale price on either side of the city line. The figures below are approximate and cover the city portion of the transfer tax only:

| Sale price | City of LA: base + ULA | Santa Monica: GS schedule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $5,300,000 | about $23,850 | about $31,800 |
| $6,000,000 | about $267,000 | about $36,000 |
| $7,900,000 | about $351,550 | about $47,400 |
| $8,000,000 | about $356,000 | $448,000 |
| $11,000,000 | about $654,500 | about $616,000 |

These figures come straight from the published rates. They are for comparison only. Your actual liability depends on deal terms, and an escrow officer or tax professional should confirm it.

At $6 million, the two sides of the line are more than $200,000 apart. At $8 million, the gap reverses. The Westside has two cliffs at two different prices, and each one changes how sellers think about pricing in a different band.

### One Line Moves Every Year. The Other Stays Put.

[The Real Deal](https://therealdeal.com/la/2026/04/10/commercial-deals-bring-in-56-percent-of-mansion-tax-revenue) reported that ULA's thresholds are indexed to inflation and that this summer they moved from $5.3 million and $10.6 million to $5.4 million and $10.9 million. Some articles from spring 2026 still quote the old numbers. Santa Monica's $8 million line is fixed for now. Under section 6.96.025 of the city code, the City Council may adjust the $8 million threshold for CPI only starting March 1, 2028, and no more than once every five years.

This matters most to an owner who bought years ago. A Brentwood home valued around $5.4 million gets a little more room under the cliff each July. A Santa Monica home approaching $8 million gets no extra room until at least 2028, even if prices keep rising.

### What a Cliff Does to an Asking Price

When a tax hits the full price, a sale just over the line can leave the seller with less money than a sale just under it. The UCLA Lewis Center saw sellers respond accordingly. Researchers Michael Manville and Jason Smith found that City of Los Angeles sales just under the original $5 million threshold ran at about three times their pre-tax share. They found a second cluster near $4.8 million, a price at which a seller could absorb some of the tax cost and still stay under the line.

Above the line, the negotiation gets harder. A luxury broker who works Sherman Oaks and Studio City told The Real Deal in July 2026 that sellers try to build the tax into their asking price. Buyers generally don't give a home more value because its seller owes a large ULA bill. That gap between asking and offering explains much of what has happened since. When neither side wants to absorb the tax, many owners decide not to sell.

### The Larger Effect Is the Listings That Don't Appear

Three studies have tried to measure this, and each uses a different method:

- UCLA Lewis Center, April 2025: an estimated 49% to 55% drop in transactions above the threshold during ULA's first 20 months. The decline was steepest for parcels other than single-family homes.

- RAND, May 28, 2026: high-value sales down an estimated 31%, plus more than 9,000 new housing units deterred through early 2026.

- Pepperdine and Beacon Economics, July 2026: monthly high-value transactions in Los Angeles down about 41% compared with surrounding jurisdictions, or roughly 1,000 fewer deals from January 2024 through March 2026. City of LA single-family prices in the $5 million-plus segment trailed nearby jurisdictions by 11% to 12%.

The ranges don't match because the studies measure different things over different periods. Pepperdine says its missing deals may include sales that were repriced below the line, moved elsewhere, delayed or dropped. A September 2025 critique from ULA supporters disputed the UCLA method. It pointed to a short post-tax period and a limited comparison group.

Building permits help show where those missing sales went. Before ULA, about 80% of Gesh Group's work was new development and 20% was remodels. Now it is about 60% remodels and 40% new builds, and many of the remodels take homes down to the studs. Levy said his remodels for homes valued above the threshold typically cost $1 million to $6 million. Many of them are in Brentwood, Bel Air, Encino and Sherman Oaks. UCLA PhD candidate Yingru Pan used ATTOM data to compare remodel permits in the two years after ULA with 2018 and 2019. She found a 46% increase for high-priced City of Los Angeles homes and no statistically significant change for mid-priced homes.

For a buyer shopping above $5.4 million in Brentwood, fewer listings is often less a sign of weak demand than of owners who chose to remodel and stay. For a move-up seller below the line, it means the pool of homes to trade up into is thinner than it would otherwise be.

### The Palisades Is Where the Rules May Change Next

Fire-destroyed lots in Pacific Palisades are selling above the ULA threshold. The Real Deal reported in August 2026 that a burned lot at 14948 Camarosa Drive sold for more than $7 million in March, 906 Glenhaven Drive sold for $6.6 million in February, and 15300 Antioch Street traded for $5.9 million in July. According to the county's damage map, the homes at all three addresses were destroyed.

City data through June shows ZIP code 90272 has generated $68.2 million in ULA revenue across 147 single-family sales since April 2023. Brentwood's 90049 has generated $125.5 million across 240 transactions.

On November 3, 2026, City of Los Angeles voters will decide Proposition TE. It would give a one-time ULA exemption or refund for residential property damaged or destroyed in the Palisades Fire. The property must be sold by whoever owned it on January 7, 2025, and the sale must close between that date and January 6, 2030. Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes the Palisades, authored the measure. She argued that taxing fire survivors as they try to recover is cruel. Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez cast the only no vote. She warned the measure could become a loophole for wealthy investors and reduce housing funds. The Housing Department projected that the exemption could cut ULA revenue by up to 6%, or $32 million a year.

TE has not passed. It also doesn't cover a whole area. It applies only to qualifying fire-damaged residential property sold by the original owner. A standing Palisades home sold by a later buyer would still fall under ULA.

### What Could Still Change Either Cliff

- The California Court of Appeal upheld ULA on December 15, 2025, rejecting the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association's challenge.

- Santa Monica won the single-subject lawsuit against Measure GS.

- A statewide Howard Jarvis initiative aimed at local transfer taxes was withdrawn in a June 2026 deal in Sacramento. Its replacement, Proposition 43, would require a two-thirds vote for future voter-initiated special taxes starting January 1, 2027. It would not change existing taxes.

- AB 736 would cap most local transfer-tax rates at 1.5%, with carve-outs that include qualifying single-family sales at or above $5.4 million. As of its last recorded action, it is still in committee after its June 25, 2026 hearing was postponed.

Until one of these changes, the rates in the table above are the ones that apply to fall 2026 closings.

### A Few Questions Sellers Ask

Does ULA apply to a home in Santa Monica?
No. ULA covers property inside City of Los Angeles limits. Santa Monica charges its own transfer tax under Measure GS.

Which ULA thresholds apply to a closing this fall?
$5.4 million and $10.9 million, for any transaction closing after June 30, 2026.

Would Proposition TE exempt every Palisades sale?
No. If voters approve it, it applies only to residential property damaged or destroyed by the fire and sold by the person who owned it on January 7, 2025, with the sale closing by January 6, 2030.

If your Westside home is valued near either threshold, the decision about whether to sell, remodel or wait comes before any pricing strategy. It helps to run those numbers with your tax advisor well before listing. Stacey Leahy can help you lay out both paths, with net proceeds on one side and remodel costs and timing on the other, so you can make the choice calmly and in private. Let's Connect.

posts.title: Los Feliz's Restaurant Boom Is a Hillhurst Story, Not a Vermont One
posts.description: Wilde's, Vandell, and the rest of Los Feliz's restaurant wave landed on Hillhurst Avenue, not Vermont. Here's what actually changed, block by block.
posts.body:
This account of Los Feliz's restaurant openings draws on [SFGATE's reporting](https://www.sfgate.com/la/article/los-feliz-restaurant-boom-21369518.php), which quoted Jeff Vance, chef and owner of Old Gold Tomato Pies: "We see people who are heading to a movie at the Vista or to the bookstore around the corner and pop in and have a slice or two." It's a small detail, but it points to something the coverage of Los Feliz's restaurant boom keeps glossing over. The boom has an address, and it isn't the street most people picture when they think of the neighborhood's commercial heart.

Outside write-ups tend to treat "Los Feliz" as one strip having one moment. Walk the actual blocks and the moment is concentrated on Hillhurst Avenue. Vermont Avenue, the street most visitors associate with the neighborhood's village character, has barely changed.

### What Actually Landed on Hillhurst

Wilde's opened at 1850 Hillhurst Avenue in late October, in the space that used to hold a Thai restaurant. It's the work of childhood friends Natasha Price, who cooks, and Tatiana Ettensberger, who runs the wine program, with chef de cuisine Sarah Durning leading a whole-hog butchery program in partnership with Peads & Barnetts. The restaurant draws on Price's British family background filtered through a California pantry, and it was [swarmed with locals from the moment it opened](https://blog.resy.com/2025/12/wildes-los-feliz/).

A few doors up the same street, Vandell opened in early December. Park Hospitality partners Michael Francesconi and Matthew Glaser built it with bar-industry veterans Shawn Lickliter and Vay Su, and Francesconi already runs Donna's and Lowboy in Echo Park, so this wasn't a team searching for its first success. He'd lived in Los Feliz for four years before opening there. The bar draws lines for its smoked tomato cocktails and cheddar-topped Wagyu burgers, and it was still pulling crowds months after opening.

Two more names from the same stretch of restaurant press round out the picture, though they sit a few blocks over on Hollywood Boulevard rather than on Hillhurst itself. Old Gold Tomato Pies, Jeff Vance's Sicilian-square pizza shop, opened on the northern side of Hollywood Boulevard the same October that Wilde's opened around the corner. Kismet, the Mediterranean restaurant Sara Kramer opened with Sarah Hymanson back in 2017, sits on Hollywood Boulevard too, with its casual sister spot Kismet Rotisserie next door since 2020. Kramer's read on the new arrivals was straightforward: more neighbors, more energy, no complaints.

### Vermont Avenue Is Coasting on What It Already Had

None of the restaurants driving this wave, Wilde's, Vandell, Old Gold, opened on Vermont Avenue. That's worth sitting with, because Vermont is the street most people picture first when they think of Los Feliz's commercial core.

What Vermont has instead is the same lineup it's had for years. The Dresden has anchored the street since 1954, the jazz-and-cocktails lounge that got a cameo in the 1996 film "Swingers" and still books live music in the same room. House of Pies keeps selling pie past midnight a few doors down. Figaro Bistrot spills its sidewalk tables out for fishbowl lattes, and Skylight Books keeps an independent bookstore running mid-block, tree growing up through the middle of the room. Every one of these has been there for years, and none of them is new.

That's not a knock on Vermont. A street that holds onto a 1954 jazz lounge and an independent bookstore for this long is doing something right. But it means the restaurant boom that outside coverage keeps describing as neighborhood-wide is really a Hillhurst Avenue story, with a couple of satellite openings a few blocks away on Hollywood Boulevard. Vermont's contribution to the story this year has mostly been staying exactly as it was.

### The Same Street Is Also Arguing With Itself

Hillhurst isn't having an uncomplicated moment, though. The same street that drew lines for Wilde's and Vandell is also where a new Philz Coffee is opening, and that news landed very differently. Philz is a chain out of Northern California, and it's arriving on a stretch of Hillhurst that already has a cluster of coffee shops within a short walk of each other. Rather than generating anything like the reaction Vandell got, [the news mostly generated a question locals are still turning over](https://laist.com/brief/news/los-angeles-activities/los-feliz-hillhurst-coffee): does this block need another coffee shop, or would something else have served the street better.

The contrast is useful because it shows the boom isn't just about newness for its own sake. A British restaurant from two friends with a specific point of view and a serious cocktail bar from operators with an established track record both read to locals as additions. A coffee chain moving into a block that already has several independent options reads as something closer to duplication. Hillhurst is absorbing both kinds of change at once, and residents are sorting them differently in real time.

### The Landmark Neither Street Can Claim

The Vista Theatre sits outside both arguments entirely. Built in 1923, the single-screen house has been owned by filmmaker Quentin Tarantino since 2021. It reopened in November 2023 after a full renovation, and true to Tarantino's stated intent when he bought it, it [screens on film rather than digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vista_Theatre_(Los_Angeles)), including 70mm prints, rather than running as a standard multiplex.

The Vista doesn't belong to Hillhurst's newer energy or to Vermont's older one. It's the kind of fixture that gives Jeff Vance's comment about customers heading to a movie before grabbing a slice its logic. People move between these streets on foot, and the theater is one of the reasons that pattern holds regardless of which strip is changing faster.

### Watch Hillhurst, Not Vermont

If you're trying to read where Los Feliz is actually moving this year, the useful question isn't what's happening in the neighborhood generally. It's what's happening on Hillhurst, because that's where nearly all of the recent restaurant and bar energy has actually landed, alongside the one addition locals are still debating. Vermont Avenue's story this year is that it didn't need to change. Both are legitimate ways for a commercial street to hold its footing, but they're different stories, and folding them into one boom narrative erases the more interesting fact: the neighborhood's two main streets are moving at completely different speeds, and the street getting all the outside attention isn't the one most people would guess.

If you spend time on Hillhurst or Vermont and have your own read on which street is actually changing, Stacey Leahy would enjoy comparing notes. Let's connect.
