posts.title: El Escorpión Park in West Hills: The Hike Your Map Gets Wrong
posts.description: A West Hills local's guide to El Escorpión Park, Hunter Allen Trail, and Shadow Ranch Park, plus why most online directions send hikers to the wrong hike.
posts.body:
Type "El Escorpion Park" into Google Maps from certain starting points in West Hills and it will try to route you to a locked gate at the end of Bell Canyon Road, inside a private community that has nothing to do with the park. Hikers who have made this mistake describe pulling up to a guard booth, getting turned around, and receiving hand-drawn directions to the actual entrance. The real trailhead sits about a tenth of a mile west of Valley Circle Boulevard on Vanowen Street, marked by a plain Los Angeles City Parks sign that reads El Scorpion Canyon Park.

That mapping error is a small thing, but it points at a bigger one. Most people who find their way to this park end up on one specific route, the technical scramble up to Castle Peak, because it is the version that shows up first in trail apps and Instagram geotags. Longtime West Hills residents rarely do that hike. They walk the easy trail next to it, or they skip the canyon altogether and drive a few minutes down the same street to Shadow Ranch Park instead. The park everyone sees online and the park locals actually use are, for practical purposes, two different places.

### The Trail Everyone Sees First

The most-reviewed route in El Escorpión Park, according to AllTrails, is Cave of Munits via El Escorpion Trail, a 1.6-mile route with 206 feet of elevation gain that ends at the mouth of a sandstone cave named for a figure in Chumash legend. Guidebooks describe this base approach as straightforward, no ropes or special gear required to reach the cave opening.

What happens after that is where the confusion starts. Hikers who continue past the cave and attempt the climb to Castle Peak, the park's 1,475-foot summit known in the Ventureño Chumash language as Kas'ele'ew, consistently describe a different experience than the cave alone suggests. Trail reviews mention hand-over-hand climbing on rock worn slick by other hikers, exposed sections with no installed rope or ladder, and more than one account of turning back partway up. The longest recorded route through this section, Castle Peak and Cave of Munits via Pressman and El Escorpion Loop, covers 4.7 miles with 895 feet of total ascent, the most elevation gain of any trail in the park. That is a legitimate scramble, not a walk with a photo opportunity at the top, and the online version of "hiking El Escorpión Park" rarely makes that distinction clear before someone is already halfway up the rock.

A trailhead sign only tells you where the park starts. It does not tell you which park you are about to enter.

### The Trail Locals Actually Walk

Set the cave and the peak aside and there is a second, much gentler trail using the same trailhead: El Escorpion Trail to Hunter Allen Trail, a 2.6-mile out-and-back with 387 feet of elevation gain that AllTrails rates as easy and estimates at just over an hour round trip. Dogs are permitted on leash. This is the out-and-back that shows up in daily foot traffic, the one dog walkers and trail runners treat as routine rather than an event worth documenting. It connects into the broader Upper Las Virgenes Canyon Open Space Preserve, so hikers who want more distance can extend the walk, but the Hunter Allen stretch itself stays flat and clear enough that it does not require the trail-finding AllTrails users mention needing on the Castle Peak approach.

The practical takeaway for anyone new to the neighborhood is that "hiking El Escorpión Park" is not one decision. It is a choice between a technical climb that draws hikers looking for a challenge and a short, dog-friendly out-and-back trail that functions more like a daily walk than an outing.

### When Shadow Ranch Makes More Sense

For a lower-effort option on the same street, Shadow Ranch Park sits at 22633 Vanowen Street, a short drive from the canyon trailhead. This park has no scrambling and no elevation to speak of. It is flat ground shaded by mature eucalyptus trees, the same trees planted in the 1800s by Alfred Workman, an Australian immigrant who bought the property in 1869 and imported Blue Gum eucalyptus from his home country. Some accounts credit the Workman Ranch groves as the origin point for much of the eucalyptus now found across California.

The property later passed to Colin Clements and Florence Ryerson, a screenwriting couple, and Ryerson co-wrote the screenplay for The Wizard of Oz while living on the ranch in the 1930s. She renamed the estate Shadow Ranch for the shade the eucalyptus canopy provided, and the Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks now runs the site as a recreation center with a playground, picnic tables, and unlighted fields for baseball, soccer, and football. It is open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Sundays. The park also hosts occasional farmers markets and craft fairs on the grounds, though nothing here requires trail shoes or a water bladder.

Here is how the four options actually compare when you line them up by what they demand rather than what they photograph well:

| Route | Distance | Elevation Gain | Difficulty | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cave of Munits via El Escorpion Trail | 1.6 mi | 206 ft | Easy to moderate | Reaching the cave mouth, turning around |
| El Escorpion Trail to Hunter Allen Trail | 2.6 mi | 387 ft | Easy | Dog walking, daily walks, trail running |
| Castle Peak and Cave of Munits Loop | 4.7 mi | 895 ft | Strenuous | Experienced hikers comfortable with off-trail scrambling |
| Shadow Ranch Park paths | Flat, no set mileage | Minimal | Easy | Shaded walking, picnics, historic site visits |

### Timing It for Fall

The Santa Monica Mountains, which El Escorpión Park backs into, are home to the Southern Pacific rattlesnake, the only venomous snake species in the range. Activity is not seasonal in the sense of disappearing on a calendar date. The Natural History Museum notes that rattlesnakes can be seen year round in Southern California, with spring and summer producing the most activity, and other trail sources place the most frequent sightings between March and October. That means by mid-September the peak has likely passed, but the tail end of the season is still in play through at least next month.

None of that rules out an early fall hike. It does argue for the same habits experienced hikers already use on the Castle Peak route: stay on the marked path where one exists, watch where hands and feet land on rock sections, and treat any warning rattle as a reason to stop and locate the sound before moving. The Natural History Museum's guidance on rattlesnake encounters is worth a read before attempting the scramble portion of the park for the first time.

A short list, if you are heading up for the first time this season:

- Confirm your map is pointed at the Vanowen Street sign, not a private gate further down Bell Canyon Road.

- Decide before you start whether you are stopping at the cave mouth or continuing to the peak. The two have very different demands.

- Keep dogs leashed on Hunter Allen Trail regardless of how quiet the path looks.

- If sturdy shoes and a hat are what you brought, that is a Hunter Allen or Shadow Ranch day, not a Castle Peak day.

### What One Trailhead Sign Says About the Neighborhood

None of this is really about hiking difficulty. It is about how much variety sits behind a single, unremarkable park sign in West Hills, and how easy it is to miss most of it because the internet only shows you the most dramatic version. The same is true a few blocks over, where a flat, shaded park built around a 19th-century ranch house offers a completely different afternoon than the canyon trail two minutes away by car. Living here long enough means learning which version of a place you actually want on a given day, rather than the one an app decided to surface first.

That kind of local pattern recognition, knowing which entrance actually gets you where you're going and which options exist just out of frame, is the same instinct that matters when someone is trying to understand a neighborhood before making a bigger decision about it. If you are thinking about property in West Hills or anywhere else in the Valley and want someone who pays attention to those details, Stacey Leahy is a good person to talk to. Let's Connect.

posts.title: Valencia's Fall Menu Isn't at the Mall Yet: What's Actually Open
posts.description: A local look at what's really new in Valencia and Old Town Newhall this fall, from CAVA and Yard House to why Round1 and KPOT are still a 2027 story.
posts.body:
Valencia Town Center has announced a bowling alley and a Korean hot pot restaurant, while other new businesses have already opened elsewhere in Valencia this year.

Centennial, the Dallas-based company that bought Valencia Town Center in 2023, announced ten new tenants on April 30, 2026: Round1 Bowling & Arcade, KPOT Korean BBQ & Hot Pot, Bushfire Kitchen, Bacio di Latte gelato, Slice House by celebrity pizzaiolo Tony Gemignani, Wafflecomb, an electronics and jewelry retailer called Trelen, the longtime Southern California skate shop Pharmacy Boardshop, and expansions for J David and Pandora. The announced tenants have different opening timelines. For local plans, the businesses and events listed below show what is already open or scheduled.

### What's already open, quietly

While Valencia Town Center works through a multi-year redevelopment, two of the year's newcomers are open somewhere else entirely.

CAVA opened its Valencia location at 27055 McBean Parkway in the Valencia Promenade shopping center in early March 2026. That's a separate property from Valencia Town Center, on the other side of McBean.

Yard House followed on April 19, 2026, taking over the former Mimi's Cafe site at the River Oaks Shopping Center on Magic Mountain Parkway. The project meant demolishing the old building and constructing a new one designed specifically for Yard House, part of an ongoing effort by city officials to refresh the River Oaks commercial corridor. If you drove past that corner earlier this year and saw fencing, that's what was going on. The corner is done now, and it's been open for months.

Neither opening was part of Valencia Town Center's redevelopment; both took place at separate properties elsewhere in Valencia.

### Valencia Town Center's opening timeline

The announced Valencia Town Center tenants are at different stages, and most have not opened yet.

Round1 is the headline addition, taking over the former Sears anchor in what would be a 125,000-square-foot entertainment complex with bowling, professional-grade billiards, karaoke, and arcade games imported from Japan, plus a planned Spo-cha sports zone and a YUU Japanese Food Hall. It's a genuinely large project. It's also, according to Round1's own March 2026 announcement and confirmed on the mall's Wikipedia entry, anticipated to open in early 2027, not this year.

The site saw little redevelopment activity for years after a 2019 plan for a Costco and luxury cinema at the former Sears location fell through in 2021. The Santa Clarita City Council approved a more flexible redevelopment framework for the roughly 111-acre mall in June 2024. By a February 2026 budget meeting, Round1 construction was underway, while the broader Town Center Specific Plan was still absent from the city's own five-year budget conversation; council members discussed ways to move redevelopment forward and asked the mall's team to identify a concrete step for the coming year.

The announced projects have different timelines. KPOT, Bushfire Kitchen, Slice House, and the rest of the April lineup came with a general window of 2026 and 2027, not confirmed dates. If your Saturday plans depend on karaoke at Round1 or hot pot at KPOT, the announced timelines don't give you a confirmed date for either.

| Business | Location | Status as of September 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CAVA | Valencia Promenade, 27055 McBean Parkway | Open since early March 2026 |
| Yard House | River Oaks Shopping Center, Magic Mountain Parkway | Open since April 19, 2026 |
| Round1 Bowling & Arcade | Valencia Town Center, former Sears site | Under construction, expected early 2027 |
| KPOT Korean BBQ & Hot Pot, Slice House, Bushfire Kitchen | Valencia Town Center | Announced April 2026, no confirmed opening date |

### Fall events in Old Town Newhall

If you want something to do this month that isn't waiting on a construction crew, Old Town Newhall has already scheduled it.

The SENSES Block Party runs on Main Street every third Thursday from April through September, and the September 17 installment goes Oktoberfest, with stein-holding contests, barrel rolling, carnival games, and an on-street bar run by The Old Town Junction. It's the last one of the season before the block party goes quiet for the winter, which makes it a real date on the calendar rather than a placeholder.

The Old Town Newhall Farmers Market runs every Saturday, year-round, rain or shine, in the Old Town Newhall Library parking lot from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. It's been running since 2015, long enough that it's less a seasonal event and more a fixture of how Saturday mornings work in this part of Santa Clarita, with small family farms and local food artisans selling produce, meats, and baked goods.

Further out, Light Up Main Street returns to Old Town Newhall on November 21 from 4 to 8 p.m., with food trucks, live entertainment, and the annual lighting of Main Street for the holidays. It's not a fall event exactly, but it's the next fixed point on the calendar after the SENSES season wraps, and it's worth marking down now if you're the type who plans around these things.

These events are scheduled for this month, while many of the mall's announced additions remain in development.

### The different timelines are the story

Here's the pattern once you line it up. Valencia Town Center's announced projects remain at different stages: Round1 is under construction, with an early 2027 opening expected, while other tenants have a general 2026 and 2027 window without confirmed dates. CAVA and Yard House are already open at separate properties. That's not a knock on Valencia Town Center's ambitions. Centennial has been explicit that it's building toward a live-work-play destination over the long run, and a 125,000-square-foot arcade and food hall inside a former anchor store is not a small lift.

But if you live here and you're wondering what changed this year, the picture has two parts. Many of the mall's announced additions remain in development, while CAVA and Yard House are open along McBean Parkway and Magic Mountain Parkway. You can walk into those restaurants this weekend, while the mall's additions continue taking shape through 2027.

If you're weighing a move to Valencia or already calling it home and want a clearer read on what's actually opening and when, Stacey Leahy pays attention to these details as part of the job, not as a side note to it. Let's Connect.

posts.title: Simi Valley's Brewery Keeps Missing Its Opening Date, Fall 2026 Guide
posts.description: Simi Valley Brewing Company has missed two opening dates while Tapo Canyon Road and East LA Avenue add new businesses. Here's what's actually happening downtown this fall.
posts.body:
The corner of Cochran and Madera has looked the same for a while now. A building that used to be a Marie Callender's, then almost became a brewery called Mad Era that never opened, now carries a different sign and a different promise. Simi Valley Brewing Company's own website still reads "Grand opening coming soon," the same four words it's carried for months, after two different target dates the company itself set.

The brewery's changing opening timeline is one example of how development is progressing at different speeds across Simi Valley, and the contrast between that corner and other parts of the city is useful context as the fall calendar fills in.

### The Brewery's Opening Timeline

In August 2025, the team behind Simi Valley Brewing Company announced plans to open in "early 2026" at 20 W. Cochran St., the long-vacant former Marie Callender's site. The project has real credentials behind it: Ali Zia, co-founder of Tarantula Hill Brewing Co. and a former executive at Bottle & Pint in Thousand Oaks, restaurateur Phil Adler of Freda's Pizza & Woodfired Kitchen, and head brewer Daniel Price, who spent years at Beachwood Brewing and Riip Beer Company. The plan calls for an 8,400-square-foot space with on-site beer production, a barbecue-focused kitchen, and room for roughly 200 people inside and another 200 on a patio shaded by oak trees.

By April 2026, that "early 2026" window had already slipped. Coverage from Hoodline and other outlets reported the team was now targeting a June opening, with the caveat that inspections and California ABC liquor licensing would ultimately decide the real date. June came and went. As of this writing in early September, the company's site still promises a grand opening is coming, without a date attached.

None of this means the project has failed. Liquor licensing and health inspections for a space this size move slowly almost everywhere, and the team has kept posting updates on Instagram as construction continues. The opening timeline has changed since its initial target. An earlier brewery at the same corner also did not open after posting construction photos for four years, with its updates ending in 2022.

"We want this to be a place where neighbors can hang out, not just drink."

A [Clair.id report](https://clair.id/2025/07/31/after-7-mad-years-of-nothing-but-a-sign-simi-valley-is-finally-getting-a-real-brewery/) quotes Ali Zia describing the vision this way. It's a good vision. The project is taking longer than the initial target suggested.

### Other Business Activity Across Simi Valley

While Cochran and Madera waits, other parts of the city have been busy. At a March 23, 2026 city council meeting, staff walked through a list of businesses already open or moving through permitting, and Mayor Dee Dee Cavanaugh specifically pointed to Whole Foods Market's confirmed arrival as a win for the community.

The rest of the list reads like a snapshot of where the city's growth is actually landing:

- Pozoleria Doña Ana, which already runs locations in the San Fernando Valley, is planning to open at 2760 Tapo Canyon Road, Suite 4

- Raising Cane's Chicken Fingers has submitted an application for 2022 First St., the former Black Bear Diner site

- The IHOP at 698 E. Los Angeles Ave. is being converted into a dual-branded concept with Applebee's, one of only a handful of such pairings in California

The listed activity spans Tapo Canyon Road, East Los Angeles Avenue, and First Street, but none of these locations is downtown.

### Two Corridors, Two Speeds

The citywide numbers back up what that address list suggests. In the first quarter of 2026, Simi Valley issued 260 business tax certificates, and unemployment dropped to 3.9% in December, lower than the county and state figures. That's genuine momentum, and it's the kind of statistic that makes a city sound like it's humming along evenly.

It isn't, quite. Industrial vacancy was 9.3%, well above the 5.5% recorded across Los Angeles County and 4.6% in Ventura County. Growth is real, but it's concentrated. Tapo Canyon Road and East Los Angeles Avenue are absorbing new tenants at a real clip. The older downtown core, where Cochran and Madera sits, is carrying a different rhythm, shaped by an aging building stock and the different timelines of brewery projects at that corner.

If you've been watching that corner hoping the citywide growth numbers meant it was about to snap into gear, the numbers themselves say otherwise. Downtown's pace and the newer corridors' pace are two separate stories that happen to share a city limit.

### Simi Valley's Fall Calendar

Simi Valley's fall lineup is already set, with most events centered on the Town Center and the Reagan Library rather than the Cochran Street corridor.

| Event | Dates | Location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simi Film Fest | September 12–20, 2026 | Studio Movie Grill, Simi Valley Town Center |
| America 250 exhibit closing | Through September 22, 2026 | Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum |
| Simi Valley Street Fair | October 24, 2026, 9 a.m.–4 p.m. | Simi Town Center Way |

The Simi Film Fest brings short films and indie features to the Studio Movie Grill inside the Town Center, with post-screening conversations built into the schedule. The Reagan Library's America 250 exhibit, tracing the country's history through the lens of Reagan's presidency, closes on September 22, which gives residents a defined window rather than an open-ended one if they've been meaning to see it. And the Street Fair returns to Simi Town Center Way on October 24 with vendors, a beer and wine garden, and a stage sponsored by Logix Federal Credit Union, according to the fair's own event listing.

These events are scheduled for the Town Center and the library, independently of the brewery project's opening timeline.

### What To Actually Watch For

If you've been following the Cochran Street storefront, the most direct updates are available from the sources closest to the project. Simi Valley Brewing Company has posted construction updates on its Instagram account. The city's economic development updates come through at council meetings roughly once a quarter, and they're where announcements like Whole Foods Market's arrival tend to surface first, well before they show up anywhere else.

For everything else on the calendar, the paths are simpler. The Street Fair and the Reagan Library exhibit both have fixed dates that aren't contingent on anyone's construction schedule. The brewery is the one variable in an otherwise settled fall.

What all of this adds up to isn't a verdict on the project itself. It's a reminder that citywide growth statistics can mask very different local rhythms, and that one project with a changing timeline does not mean the surrounding streets have stopped growing. Tapo Canyon Road and East Los Angeles Avenue are proving that point every time a new tenant sign goes up. Cochran and Madera will get there. It's just moving on its own clock.

If you're weighing a move to Simi Valley, or already live here and are thinking about what a home in this market actually looks like right now, Stacey Leahy can walk you through it with the same attention to detail as everything above. Let's Connect.

posts.title: The Promenade Went Quiet: Where Woodland Hills Actually Spends Its Weekend Now
posts.description: A look at how Woodland Hills' daily routines have shifted to Topanga Village and Ventura Boulevard, plus the three farmers markets, free summer concerts, and trail most residents overlook.
posts.body:
For years, the Promenade was the default answer to "what should we do tonight." The food court, the multiplex, the low-stakes Saturday that didn't require a plan. Then the fencing went up, and it stayed up, and the 34-acre lot became the kind of landmark you drive past without really registering anymore.

If your Saturday routine still starts by pointing the car toward that stretch of Topanga Canyon Boulevard out of habit, it's worth checking whether the plan has quietly relocated without telling you.

### The Fenced Lot Finally Got an Answer

The Promenade's 34 acres sat as an open question for years after the mall closed. That changed last year, when Rams owner Stan Kroenke's organization unveiled plans for Rams Village at Warner Center, a 52-acre mixed-use project combining the old Promenade site with the neighboring former Anthem Blue Cross parcel. The plan calls for the Rams' permanent headquarters and training facility, two indoor entertainment venues, a retail village, and roughly 3,000 homes, with construction on the permanent buildings targeted to begin in 2027 and run for up to a decade. Demolition of the old mall structure is already underway. None of that changes anything about this weekend, though. A build-out that stretches toward the mid-2030s means the practical question for anyone living here now isn't what the Promenade eventually becomes. It's where people are already going instead, tonight.

That question has an answer, and it's sitting right across the street.

### Topanga Village Absorbed the Habit Before the Site Plan Was Final

Across the street from the fenced lot, Topanga Village has been quietly doing the work the Promenade used to do. The center runs over 500,000 square feet with more than 80 stores and restaurants, anchored by a Costco that ranks among the highest performing in the country. The food lineup there now reads less like a mall directory and more like a compact downtown:

- Alfred Coffee

- Bacio di Latte

- Cava

- Dan Modern Chinese

- EMC Seafood

- Eureka!

- Il Fornaio

- Joey's Woodland Hills

- Kabob Village

- Larsen's Steakhouse

- Modern Bread and Bagel

- Pitfire Pizza

- Pressed Juicery

- Protini Bar

- Saint & Second

- Sloan's

- Sushi Katsu-ya

The most telling name on that list is Saint & Second. The Long Beach and Manhattan Beach group opened its third location in the space that used to be Lucille's Smokehouse Bar-B-Que, bringing a chef-driven seasonal menu, a curated wine list, and a spacious patio built around a fire pit. It has become one of the busier reservations in the neighborhood since opening, and it is doing that business in a building people used to walk past on their way to Lucille's ribs.

A large second-generation restaurant space still sits open near Joey's and Coffee Bean, along with a former Veggie Grill corner already built out with a hood and grease interceptor. That is not a fully leased shopping center. It's one with room for two or three more restaurants before Rams Village breaks ground next door, which suggests the Topanga Village lineup will keep shifting through the rest of the year rather than settling into place.

A few minutes west, on Ventura Boulevard, chef David Gussin opened his first brick-and-mortar restaurant, Prose Kitchen & Bar, at 21150 Ventura Boulevard, after years cooking at STK, Fig & Olive, and Cleo. The 60-plus seat dining room is paired with an all-season patio, complete with heat lamps and cooling misters, that seats another 30 guests year-round. Danny Boy's Pizza also opened its third location in the neighborhood this year, a counter inside the Valley Country Market at 20929 Ventura Boulevard, bringing New York-style slices, Sicilian squares, and garlic knots to a corner of the west side that hadn't had a casual pizza spot in a while.

None of this required the Promenade to be resolved. It happened around it.

### Three Farmers Markets, and Most People Only Know the One

Ask a Woodland Hills resident where the farmers market is and you'll usually get one answer, when there are three running on three different days with three different personalities.

| Market | Day & Hours | Location | Character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Woodland Hills Farmers' Market | Saturday, 9am–1:30pm | 5650 Shoup Ave | Year-round, 30-plus vendors, live music, kids' activities, a knife-sharpening booth, and rotating specialty vendors selling jams, pickles, and olive oil |
| Warner Center Farmers' Market | Wednesday, 10am–2pm | 5820 Canoga Ave | Smaller midweek stop, easy to fold into a lunch break in the office corridor |
| Kaiser Permanente Farmers' Market | Thursday, 9am–2pm | 5601 De Soto Ave, inside the Kaiser campus | Built for staff and patients, but open to anyone passing through |

The Saturday market at Shoup Avenue is the one that shows up on Nextdoor and gets the recurring updates about returning vendors and weekend specials. The other two run quietly enough that even longtime residents are sometimes surprised to learn a Wednesday or Thursday option exists at all. If your week only has room for one grocery run outside a regular store, picking the day that matches your schedule rather than defaulting to Saturday is worth the five minutes it takes to check.

### The Sunday Anchor That Didn't Move All Summer

While the restaurant map has been shifting, one fixture in Woodland Hills held completely still. The Valley Cultural Foundation's free Sunday concert series at Warner Park ran from June 14 through August 23 this year, with performances at the Nora Ross Bandshell inside the Lou Bredlow Pavilion at 5800 Topanga Canyon Boulevard. Shows started at 5:30pm with an emerging local act, followed by a headline tribute band, and wrapped by 8pm, leaving room for a picnic on the lawn before the sun went down.

That run just ended. The free weekly excuse to end up at Warner Park has gone quiet until next June. If you've been eating at Topanga Village anyway, the short walk east to the park after dinner was, during the concert run this summer, a preview of the kind of walkable evening Rams Village is promising once it's finally built, just already working today.

### One Walk Worth Adding to the Rotation

If Sunday nights need a new anchor now that the concerts have wrapped, Serrania Ridge Trail is a reasonable substitute. It's a 2.3-mile out-and-back climb with about 456 feet of elevation gain, starting at the dedicated lot on Wells Drive and ending at a bench near Mulholland Drive with a clear view over the San Fernando Valley. Dogs are welcome, and off-leash in some stretches, which is part of why it functions as an unofficial dog park as much as a hiking trail. The climb has almost no shade, so it rewards an early morning or a late-day start when the light is better anyway, and the bench at the top has become the unofficial spot for watching the sun drop behind the Santa Monica Mountains.

### What This Actually Adds Up To

None of these pieces are dramatic on their own. A new restaurant here, a market schedule most people only half know, a concert season that ends on schedule every August. Put together, they describe a neighborhood whose center of gravity has already moved from the Promenade to the Topanga Village and Ventura corridor, well before the fenced lot's new future is anything more than a rendering. The habits that used to route toward the food court are worth updating now, not in ten years when the construction is finished.

I spend a lot of my time in Woodland Hills paying attention to exactly this kind of shift, because it tells you as much about a neighborhood as any listing does. If you're curious about what else has changed around here, or you'd like to talk about property in the area for any reason at all, I'd love to hear from you. You can find me at Stacey Leahy.

posts.title: Encino's Sunday Routine Runs on Two Different Clocks
posts.description: A local's guide to how an Encino weekend actually unfolds, from the ONEgeneration Farmers Market and Sepulveda Basin Dog Park to Heritage Days at Los Encinos State Historic Park and dinner on Ventura Boulevard.
posts.body:
Ask a longtime Encino resident what they're doing this Sunday and you'll usually get some version of the same answer: farmers market in the morning, maybe the dog park, dinner on the boulevard if the week wasn't too much. It sounds like one easy loop. It isn't. Encino's weekend actually splits into two separate clusters that sit on the same north-south spine, Balboa Boulevard, but run on different clocks entirely, and most people only ever experience one of them on a given Sunday without realizing the other exists a few miles up the same street.

That gap matters more than it sounds like it should, because one of those clusters only turns on once a month.

### The Basin Loop: Weekly, Reliable, Built Around a Nonprofit

Head north on Balboa and you land in the flatter, quieter stretch near the Sepulveda Basin, where the ONEgeneration Encino Farmers Market has been running every Sunday, rain or shine, from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. at 17400 Victory Boulevard, between White Oak and Balboa. During the peak growing months between May and November, roughly 40 farms set up here, with about a third of them certified organic, alongside a fish monger, two bakeries, and vendors selling everything from grass-fed beef to handmade soap. The market isn't a private venture. It's run by ONEgeneration, the local senior services nonprofit, and a share of every dollar spent there goes toward homebound meals, transportation for frail seniors, and four lunch sites for low-income older adults in the San Fernando Valley. Shopping there on a Sunday morning is, in a small and unglamorous way, also how the neighborhood funds part of its senior care network.

A short walk from the market is the Sepulveda Basin Off-Leash Dog Park, a 6.5-acre space split into three sections for large dogs, small dogs, and a dedicated training area, so a nervous terrier isn't sharing a section with a Lab that wants to sprint. It's open daily, but there's one detail that trips up newcomers: the park closes every Friday morning from 6 to 11 a.m. for maintenance. Show up on a Friday before eleven expecting the usual crowd and you'll find a locked gate instead. It's a small scheduling quirk, but it's exactly the kind of thing you only know if you've actually been there, not if you've just read that Encino "has a nice dog park."

### The Boulevard Loop: Older, Slower, and Easy to Drive Past

Head back south toward Ventura Boulevard and the neighborhood changes register entirely. A block off Ventura, at 16756 Moorpark Street, sits Los Encinos State Historic Park, which most drivers pass without a second look. It's easy to underestimate. The park occupies the site of Siutcanga, a village inhabited by Tongva, Chumash, and Tataviam people that predates the Spanish arrival, and it still holds the original nine-room De la Ossa Adobe, built in 1849, along with the two-story stone Garnier Building, a working blacksmith shop, and a natural spring that once supplied year-round water to the village itself. On Fridays, the park runs free guided walking tours covering how the natural springs, Indigenous history, and the Gold Rush shaped Encino's transition from Mexican rancho land to American California. But the detail that actually changes the experience is Heritage Days: on the third Sunday of every month, from 1 to 3 p.m., the blacksmith shop opens for live demonstrations of rancho-era metalsmithing. Visit on any other Sunday and the shop stays closed. Visit on the third Sunday, and you get a working glimpse of a trade that's otherwise just a locked building with a placard.

A few minutes away on Ventura Boulevard itself, the boulevard loop has picked up a genuinely new stop this year. Popular, the seventh concept from the Tel Aviv Restaurant Group, opened at 18047 Ventura Boulevard in early 2026 under Executive Chef Dor Priezler, serving Mediterranean fusion with a seafood-forward menu, dishes like a branzino-filled Fish Cigar, and a cocktail bar built for evening crowds. Since opening, it has expanded into breakfast and brunch service as well, adding Tel Aviv and Israeli breakfast plates and avocado toast to a boulevard that's historically been stronger on dinner than daytime options. For residents who already treat Ventura Boulevard as their default stretch for a night out, that's a real shift, not just another restaurant added to a long list.

### Why the Two Loops Rarely Overlap

Part of the reason so few people string these together into one day is that they genuinely don't share a rhythm. Here's how the cadence actually breaks down:

| Stop | Day | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ONEgeneration Farmers Market | Sunday | Weekly, year-round |
| Sepulveda Basin Dog Park | Daily | Closed Friday 6 to 11 a.m. |
| History Walking Tours | Friday | Weekly |
| Heritage Days Blacksmith Demo | Third Sunday | Monthly |
| Popular (Ventura Blvd) | Daily | Now serving breakfast through dinner |

The only day these calendars actually line up is the third Sunday of the month, when the farmers market, the dog park, and the blacksmith demonstration are all running at once, on opposite ends of the same boulevard. Every other Sunday, a resident who assumes the historic park is "always doing something" will show up to a quiet adobe and a locked blacksmith shop, because the walking tours happen on Fridays and the live demonstration only happens twelve times a year.

None of this is a criticism of the neighborhood. If anything, it's the opposite. Encino isn't thin on things to do. It's just organized in a way that rewards people who've lived here long enough to know the schedule, rather than people skimming a generic list of neighborhood highlights. A market that funds senior meal delivery, a state park sitting on top of a 4,000-year-old village site, and a restaurant scene that's finally filling in its breakfast hours don't read as a single cohesive itinerary from the outside. They read that way once you've actually done the loop enough times to know which Sunday is which.

### Building an Actual Encino Sunday

If you're trying to catch everything worth seeing in one weekend rather than stumbling into it by accident, here's what that looks like in practice:

- Check the calendar first. If it's the third Sunday of the month, the blacksmith shop at Los Encinos State Historic Park will be open from 1 to 3 p.m., which is the only time it runs.

- Hit the farmers market early. It runs 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. every Sunday at 17400 Victory Boulevard, and the better produce and prepared food tend to move fast in the first couple of hours.

- Give the dog park a pass on Friday mornings before 11 a.m. Any other time, it's open.

- Save Fridays for the walking tour if the history side interests you more than the blacksmith demo specifically.

- End on Ventura Boulevard. Popular now covers the day from breakfast through dinner, which wasn't true a year ago.

None of this requires becoming an expert in local infrastructure. It just requires knowing that a neighborhood this settled doesn't actually run on one clock, it runs on several, and the difference between a good Sunday and a slightly disappointing one usually comes down to whether you checked which Sunday it was before you left the house.

If you're the kind of person who likes knowing a neighborhood this well before you ever think about buying or selling in it, that's exactly the kind of local detail Stacey Leahy pays attention to, not because it moves a transaction forward, but because it's the difference between knowing a place and just living near it. When the time comes to talk about Encino as more than a Sunday routine, Let's Connect.

posts.title: What Changed on Riverside Drive in Toluca Lake This Year
posts.description: A resident's look at what's new on Toluca Lake's Riverside Drive in 2026, from Gelson's to Akami Sushi to Flour Pizzeria, and why the village is getting denser, not bigger.
posts.body:
Walk the two blocks of Riverside Drive between Cahuenga and Forman on any weekday around noon and the sidewalk tells you something the storefronts don't say out loud. Two new businesses have opened on Riverside Drive since January. A grocery store moved into a spot that used to hold a sports bar and a post office, and a sushi restaurant took over a room that used to be a different sushi restaurant. A third arrival, Flour Pizzeria, is preparing to open at 4201 W. Alameda Avenue, in a space that used to sell pizza under another name.

That pattern is the story. Toluca Lake's village core isn't expanding outward. It's getting denser inside the same footprint it has held for years, and the reason has less to do with taste and more to do with math: this stretch of Riverside sits five minutes from Warner Bros., closer still to Universal, and a short light from Disney, which means the lunch and after-work crowd here has never been limited by who lives in the neighborhood. It's limited by seat count. Taken together, the openings read as an answer to that limit, not a bet on something new.

### What Opened or Is Opening This Year

Here's the plain accounting, address by address, as of this writing.

| Business | Address | Status as of August 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gelson's (small-format) | 10067 Riverside Drive at Mariota Avenue | Opened January 28, 2026 |
| Akami Sushi (second location) | 10658 Riverside Drive, former Sushi Ran space | Open |
| Flour Pizzeria & Cafe | 4201 W. Alameda Avenue, former Slices space | Preparing to open |

Two swaps on the strip. Zero net new square footage on the strip. If you've lived here for any stretch of time, that's the detail worth sitting with before you get to what's actually on the menu.

### A Second Chair at the Sushi Counter

Akami Sushi is the more interesting of the three, because it didn't have to come here. The restaurant is a small, suburban operator with one prior location in Arcadia, and Toluca Lake was its first attempt at a second address anywhere. According to [Akami's own site](https://akami-sushi.com/), the restaurant is helmed by owner Jeffry Undiarto, who spent more than twelve years working in Los Angeles kitchens including the two-Michelin-starred n/naka before opening the Arcadia location with his sister Jennifer and her husband Andy. That's a chef with options choosing a two-block strip in the Valley over any number of easier trade areas.

The choice makes more sense once you look at what was already here. Sushi Yuzu, a few doors down, runs a handroll counter with a real waitlist on most nights. It has already spun off a second concept on the same corridor, Kabosu. Yunomi Handroll sits nearby too. That's three sushi counters within a short walk before Akami ever opened its doors, which on paper reads like oversupply. In practice, a second sit-down sushi option doesn't have to steal from Sushi Yuzu's line. It just gives the block somewhere to put the overflow. Akami is open now for lunch and dinner daily, and the addition reads less like competition and more like the market finally building a second door for a line that was already forming.

### The Pizza Import

Flour Pizzeria & Cafe is the harder case to explain, because Brentwood and Toluca Lake aren't neighbors and don't share an obvious customer base. Flour has run a single location on San Vicente Boulevard for years without expanding anywhere. The move into the former Slices space on West Alameda Avenue, a short walk from the Warner Bros. lot, is the brand's first step outside the Westside entirely.

The read here is the same one as for Akami: proximity to three studio lots may keep daily demand for a fast, reliable lunch running higher than the existing seat count can absorb. A New York-style slice near the Warner gate fits that reading.

### A Grocery Store Sized for a Village

As [Patch reported](https://patch.com/california/los-angeles/gelsons-open-new-small-format-store-toluca-lake), the Gelson's that opened on January 28 is the anchor of the three, and its size tells you something the ribbon-cutting photos don't. At 9,672 square feet, the new store is less than half the size of the chain's original 1951 flagship, a 25,000-square-foot store that opened at Hollywood Way and Victory Boulevard in Burbank, on a site that's a Petco today. Gelson's operates more than two dozen stores across Los Angeles and Orange counties, and for this corner it opened a small-format market.

The store sits on the ground floor of a new building called The Ambrea, which holds 37 apartment units above the retail space. The site wasn't vacant land before construction. A well-known outdoor sports bar, Michael's on Riverside, came down to make room for it, and the neighborhood's post office relocated off that same stretch. The project moved forward under transit-oriented zoning, a detail some residents raised during the approval process, since the closest bus stop that would qualify doesn't actually serve a route inside Toluca Lake proper, only just over the line in Burbank. None of that changes what opened. It does explain why a low-rise village absorbed its first mixed-use building in years: this was the trade that had to happen for a grocery store to land on a block that otherwise has no room left to build.

On opening day, Gelson's made donations to three local institutions: the Garry Marshall Theatre, Pawsitive Beginnings LA, and Toluca Lake Elementary School. A theater, a rescue, and a school is not a random list. It's a company reading exactly who eats, walks, and sends their kids to school within a ten-minute radius of that corner.

### The Corners That Didn't Move

For every new name on the block, the businesses that have anchored Toluca Lake for years are still exactly where they were.

- Verse, the Riverside Drive supper club owned by a Grammy-winning sound mixer, still books live music every night, not as a rotating special but as the standing plan.

- Sushi Yuzu still runs its handroll counter with a wait even after you join the online list.

- Forman's still handles the lunch rush with a burger that regulars plan around.

- Don Cuco is still where the after-work margarita crowd lands.

- Bodega Malbec still holds the best outdoor tables on the strip for an Argentinian dinner.

- Toluca Bakery, a family-run, all-vegan bakery near Riverside and Camarillo Street, is still turning out conchas, tamales, and a tres leches cake regulars have been ordering for years.

None of these had to compete for space with the new arrivals, because none of the new arrivals were built to replace them. They filled a gap the old guard didn't cover: a faster grocery run, a second sushi seat, a closer slice.

### What the Compression Actually Means

The easy version of this story is "Toluca Lake has two new businesses open and a third preparing to open." The more accurate one is that a village with almost no room left to grow found a way to get more useful without getting any bigger. The ten-minute walk down Riverside Drive now covers a wider set of errands than it did in December because the two Riverside arrivals added options within the same footprint; Flour is preparing to open on West Alameda Avenue. A sports bar became a grocery store. One sushi kitchen became two. A pizza spot that used to sell pizza under a different name is about to sell pizza again, just from a brand with a track record.

If you've lived here through a few cycles of turnover, that's worth noticing on its own terms, independent of anything it might mean for property values or timing. The block you already know how to walk just got a little more efficient at being itself.

If you're the kind of person who likes knowing why a neighborhood changes shape and not just that it did, Stacey Leahy spends her weeks walking blocks exactly like this one across the Valley. Let's Connect if you'd ever like to talk through what's actually happening on a specific street, in Toluca Lake or anywhere nearby.

posts.title: Studio City's Restaurant Boom Is Full of Repeat Players, Not Rookies
posts.description: A resident's guide to what's new on Studio City's Ventura Boulevard, and why so many of the openings are expansions from operators who already succeeded elsewhere.
posts.body:
Have you noticed how many of the new signs on Ventura Boulevard belong to people who already had a restaurant somewhere nearby?

It is easy to read the last year and a half on this stretch of the boulevard as a simple wave of new openings, and there have been a lot of them. But look closer at who is actually behind the storefronts, and a different pattern shows up. This is not a corridor full of first-time operators testing an idea to see if it sticks. It is a corridor where people who already know Studio City, or who already succeeded somewhere else in Los Angeles, decided this particular stretch was worth their next move. That distinction matters if you live here, because it tells you something about how the neighborhood actually reads to the people whose job is to guess where Angelenos want to eat.

### Follow the Names, Not Just the Signage

Rosetta Osteria and Crudo Bar took over the former Village space at 12345 Ventura Boulevard with a coastal Italian menu built around hamachi, branzino, and Hokkaido scallops. The name behind it is Frank Leon, a longtime Studio City restaurateur sometimes called the Mayor of Studio City, who already runs Leona's nearby. Leona's has a Michelin Plate. Rosetta is not a stranger placing a bet on an unfamiliar block. It is an established local operator doubling down on the same few miles of Ventura Boulevard where his other restaurant already works.

Highly Likely, the all-day cafe with the old-school diner look and a menu that runs from Japanese breakfast bowls to steak frites at dinner, is not a debut either. It is the concept's fourth location, meaning three other neighborhoods already proved it out before Studio City got a turn.

And then there is [Little Lenny's](https://www.opentable.com/r/lennys-casita-los-angeles), the kosher Mexican counter at 11923 Ventura Boulevard. It is a spinoff, not a startup, built by the team behind Lenny's Casita on West Pico Boulevard. Co-owner Gil Tsruya told What Now Los Angeles the goal was to take a proven menu and make it work for a wider audience.

"Over the years we wanted to expand, but in a way that was open also for non-kosher customers," Tsruya said.

That is a business already confident in its food, choosing Studio City as the place to widen its reach rather than the place to figure itself out.

### What a Proven Operator's Bet Actually Looks Like

Once you notice that pattern, the shape of the new wave starts to make more sense. Alto Fire to Table did not open as a casual concept with room to adjust later. It arrived as a dinner-only, reservation-based room built around a fully open-flame kitchen, where dry-aged steaks and traditional chipa and criollo breads come with tableside cocktail service. That is a full commitment to an occasion, not a soft launch.

Great White leans the opposite direction, spanning breakfast through dinner as a coastal Californian all-day spot, which is its own kind of confidence. Running a kitchen from morning coffee through evening cocktails takes a different staffing and supply chain than a dinner-only room, and it only pencils out if you already believe there is foot traffic on the boulevard at every hour, not just at 7 p.m.

The same logic shows up in the smaller, quieter openings. Cafe Matcha and Omake, a coffee and tea tasting room, are not trying to out-shout Alto or Rosetta. They are betting that the boulevard has room for a slower, more ceremony-minded stop between the bigger destinations, which is a different kind of local read than assuming every new opening needs to be the loudest one on the block.

### A Fifteen-Minute Walk, Door to Door

Almost all of this sits inside a walk you can do without moving your car, roughly between Vineland Avenue and Coldwater Canyon Avenue. If you are mapping out where to go this week, here is what that stretch actually looks like right now:

- Alto Fire to Table, open-flame Argentine steak, dinner only, reservations recommended

- Rosetta Osteria and Crudo Bar, coastal Italian from Frank Leon, opening into a late-night bar scene

- Little Lenny's, kosher Mexican counter service, closed Friday afternoon through Saturday sundown

- Vignette, a California bistro in the old Vintage Wine and Eats space that sources produce from the Sunday farmers market

- The Last Canteen, an immersive, post-apocalyptic cocktail bar near Vineland with sarsaparilla on draft, in the space that used to be Gray Tavern

- Highly Likely, all-day diner-style cafe, its fourth location

- Cafe Matcha and Omake, specialty coffee and a quieter tea tasting room

That is open-flame steak, coastal Italian, kosher Mexican, a farmers-market bistro, a themed cocktail bar, an all-day diner, and two specialty coffee and tea rooms, all within a walk you could do in one evening if you wanted to.

### The Old Guard Underneath the New Wave

None of this is replacing what made Studio City a dining neighborhood in the first place. Sushi Row, the run of Japanese restaurants along the same corridor, has been there for decades. Katsu-ya has been open since 1997. Teru Sushi has been open since 1979. Asanebo holds a Michelin star. The new wave is building on top of a foundation that was already unusually deep for a suburban boulevard, not replacing it.

Little Lenny's schedule is its own kind of evidence for that same point. A restaurant that closes Friday afternoon and reopens Saturday after sundown is not chasing a trend cycle. That same long-standing rhythm is visible at [the Studio City Farmers Market](https://www.studiocityfarmersmarket.com/), which has run every Sunday for years on Ventura Place between Laurel Canyon Boulevard and Radford Avenue as a nonprofit jointly run by the Studio City Chamber of Commerce Foundation and the Studio City Residents Association. New restaurants come and go faster than either of those things. What they are opening around has been stable for a long time.

### Retail Is Making the Same Bet

The pattern is not limited to restaurants. Marine Layer, the coastal apparel brand, opened at [The Shops at Sportsmen's Lodge](https://www.shopsatsportsmenslodge.com/) in late May 2026, adding to a center that already anchors its retail lineup with Erewhon, the only location of that grocer in the San Fernando Valley, and Equinox. The Shops sit on the site of the old Sportsmen's Lodge hotel, a former Hollywood watering hole once frequented by Clark Gable, John Wayne, and Bette Davis, redeveloped into a 95,000-square-foot open-air center. A national apparel brand choosing to open its next store at the eastern gateway of this same corridor is the retail version of Highly Likely picking Studio City for its fourth location. Somebody ran the numbers on foot traffic here and liked what they saw.

### What Is Not Open Yet

At least one more signal is still in progress. Pop Up Bagels is coming soon to 12184 Ventura Boulevard, an East Coast import filling one of the last open storefronts in this stretch. Watching who eventually takes that space, and any others that turn over next, will tell you whether the pattern holds: another proven name from somewhere else, betting that Studio City is where it makes its next move.

If you already live here, none of this requires a decision from you beyond which direction to walk on a Sunday after the farmers market lets out. But it is worth knowing that the people opening these doors are not guessing. They have already done this somewhere else, successfully, and they picked your boulevard for the next round.

If you are ever curious about what any of this means for property values, timing, or your own plans in Studio City, Stacey Leahy is always glad to talk it through. Let's Connect.

posts.title: Why Valley Village's Median Price Is Falling While Studio City's Climbs
posts.description: Valley Village's median home price is down while Studio City's is up. The real driver isn't the neighborhood, it's California's SB 326 balcony law and what it means for condo buyers in 2026.
posts.body:
Two weeks ago I toured a single-family ranch on a quiet residential street in Valley Village, then drove four minutes to see a two-bedroom condo built in roughly the same era near the Burbank Boulevard corridor. Similar age. Similar square footage. The kind of pairing a buyer comparing Valley Village to Studio City on paper might treat as interchangeable data points feeding into one neighborhood median.

They are not interchangeable right now. The ranch would have sold for more than it did a year ago. The condo came with an HOA binder documenting a required structural inspection, a pending special assessment vote, and a note that the building's financing status was under lender review.

That difference, repeated across a neighborhood that mixes single-family homes with a real share of condos, townhomes, and small multifamily buildings, is what shows up in the data as Valley Village's falling median.

### The Number Everyone's Quoting

Pull up Valley Village on any portal this summer and the headline repeats itself in different fonts. Redfin data for the three months ending May 2026 puts the median sale price at $1.1 million, down 9.87 percent from the same period a year earlier, with median price per square foot down 10.1 percent over the same stretch. Zillow's typical home value for the neighborhood sat at $1,176,651 as of May 31, 2026, down 7.5 percent year over year. Movoto's July 2026 figures show a $1.19 million median list price, still trending down month over month.

Four minutes away, Studio City tells the opposite story. Redfin data for the first quarter of 2026 put that neighborhood's median sale price around $1.93 million, up roughly 18.5 percent year over year, with homes averaging 56 days on market and closing near a 98 percent sale-to-list ratio. Other sources place Studio City's median closer to $1.62 million, with Zillow's typical value lower still, near $1.5 million. That spread is a reminder that portal medians depend heavily on which slice of inventory each site is sampling in a given month, worth keeping in mind before treating any single figure as settled fact.

Even allowing for that noise, the direction holds across sources: Valley Village is down and Studio City is up, although the figures cover different reporting periods. Buyers frequently cross-shop both.

### One Neighborhood, Two Housing Markets

The instinct is to read that gap as a verdict on the neighborhood itself, evidence that Studio City is pulling ahead while Valley Village slips as the more affordable option next door. The property-type data tells a narrower and more useful story.

Recent market figures for Valley Village show single-family homes selling for an average of $1.36 million more than condos, which is expected given the size difference. What matters is the direction each segment is moving. Single-family sale prices rose 4.7 percent month over month in the same window that condo sale prices fell 30.1 percent. Single-family homes sold roughly 0.90 percent below list price on average. Condos sold slightly above list, at 0.25 percent, yet sat on the market 72 days longer than single-family homes did.

Read together, that is not a neighborhood in decline. It is a neighborhood where two products sharing a zip code and almost nothing else in cost structure are being priced by two different buyer pools for two different reasons. Valley Village's housing stock spans single-family ranches, Spanish-style homes, character properties, remodeled traditionals, newer construction, condos, townhomes, and small multifamily buildings. A median built from that mix will move whenever the balance between those categories shifts, even when no individual home has actually lost value.

A buyer comparing Valley Village to Studio City on median price alone is often comparing a condo market to a single-family market without realizing it.

### Why 2026 Is the Year This Shows Up

The condo softness is not random timing. January 1, 2026 was the statewide deadline under [California's SB 326](https://www.lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/preparing-for-2026-hoa-law-changes-homeowners-guide) for condominium HOAs with three or more units to complete a first inspection of exterior elevated elements, meaning balconies, decks, and walkways six feet or higher that are substantially supported by wood. The law traces back to the 2015 Berkeley balcony collapse and had already been pushed back once, from an original 2025 deadline, because of an inspector shortage. There was no more room to push it again.

The inspections are surfacing exactly the deferred maintenance older buildings tend to carry. HOA attorney Jeff Beaumont of Beaumont Tashjian has [reported insurance premiums rising 100 to 400 percent](https://governingdocs.dev/blog/california-sb-326-balcony-law/) in affected buildings, with special assessments reaching as high as $175,000 per unit in extreme cases and a more common range for major repair work running $40,000 to $60,000 per unit. Lenders have started requesting SB 326 certification as part of underwriting, and buildings that fail a warrantability review push buyers toward non-warrantable financing, which according to [reporting on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac standards](https://www.mortgagegrader.com/blog/californias-balcony-law-and-fannie-mae-standards-could-push-condo-fees-higher) runs roughly 1.25 percentage points higher in rate and typically requires at least 20 percent down instead of as little as 3 percent.

None of that touches a detached house. A single-family home doesn't have a shared roof, a shared balcony, or a master insurance policy a carrier can reprice overnight. That is the mechanism. Buyers haven't soured on Valley Village. A meaningful share of its inventory now carries a cost and financing risk that didn't show up in last year's numbers, while Studio City's inventory, which skews overwhelmingly single-family, doesn't carry it at all.

### What to Check Before You Write an Offer on a Valley Village Condo

None of this means avoiding condos in the neighborhood. It means due diligence has more steps than it did two years ago. Before getting attached to a unit, ask for:

- The building's SB 326 inspection report, or confirmation of when it's scheduled

- The current reserve study, updated to reflect any inspection findings

- A certificate of insurance showing the current premium and any carrier-flagged coverage gaps

- Any special assessment votes scheduled or already approved

- Confirmation from your lender that the building meets Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac warrantability standards, since that determines your rate and required down payment

A seller's agent should be able to produce most of this before contingencies come off. If they can't, that tells you something too.

### What This Means Pocket by Pocket

Valley Village isn't one market even within its own borders. The Burbank Boulevard side leans toward condos, townhomes, and small multifamily buildings alongside single-family homes, which makes it the pocket most exposed to the SB 326 repricing described above. The streets on the southwestern side, closer to Ventura Boulevard, compete more directly with Studio City and skew more heavily single-family, which likely explains why that pocket tracks closer to Studio City's trend than the neighborhood-wide median suggests. The eastern side, near the NoHo Arts District, the Metro, the 170 freeway, and Universal City, draws a different buyer entirely, one prioritizing connectivity over land, where a condo's lower entry price can still make sense once a building's finances check out.

Deciding between Valley Village and Studio City based on a headline median means deciding between three sub-markets and a coin flip on building finances without realizing it. Narrowing to your actual property type before comparing medians gets you a real answer instead of a misleading one.

### Reading the Studio City Comparison Correctly

Studio City's climbing median isn't a mystery once you factor in what's actually selling there. It carries far less condo and multifamily inventory relative to Valley Village, so it isn't absorbing the SB 326 shock the same way. Layer in [the Residences at Sportsmen's Lodge](https://www.cbsnews.com/losangeles/news/la-city-leaders-approve-redevelopment-project-at-sportsmens-lodge/), a 520-unit project at Ventura and Coldwater that the Los Angeles City Council approved in 2024 with completion expected in 2027, and you have a corridor where new retail and residential density is building on top of a market already dominated by detached homes. That momentum doesn't cancel out what's happening one zip code over in Valley Village's condo stock. It means the two neighborhoods are responding to different forces, not that one is winning and the other is losing.

### A Few Questions Buyers Ask

Does SB 326 apply if I'm buying a townhome instead of a condo?
It depends on the structure, not the label. SB 326 applies to condominium-form HOAs with three or more units where balconies, decks, or walkways are wood-supported and six feet or higher off the ground. Confirm which category your building falls under before assuming either way.

Will Valley Village condo prices keep falling?
Deferred inspections, resulting assessments, and insurance repricing tend to play out over twelve to twenty-four months as buildings work through compliance and settle their finances. Buildings that clear SB 326 requirements and update their reserves should stabilize faster than ones still working through the process. There's no way to time that precisely, which is why the due diligence list above matters more than the headline number ever will.

Should I rule out Valley Village if I want a single-family home?
The data argues the opposite. The single-family segment was still appreciating in the same window the overall median fell, and pockets bordering Studio City's Ventura Boulevard side compete closely with it on price per square foot without needing to absorb the condo-specific headwinds described here.

Buying or selling in Valley Village, Studio City, or anywhere between them right now means reading past the headline number to the property type underneath it. If you want a second read on a specific listing, or want to understand what a building's HOA financials actually say before you write an offer, Stacey Leahy can walk through it with you. posts.title: Burbank in August 2026: New Downtown Openings Meet the Festival Calendar
posts.description: A Burbank resident's guide to August 2026: how new Downtown openings like Tigawok, Flow Wine & Coffee, and Chubby Dumpling reshape the walk between the Film Festival, Comedy Festival, Starlight Bowl, and Magnolia Park.
posts.body:
For years, August in Burbank meant picking one thing. You went to the film festival or you went to Starlight Bowl. You caught a Candlelight concert at the Equestrian Center or you did Food Truck Friday on Magnolia. This August is the first time the map argues for stacking them, because the blocks between the venues have quietly filled in with places worth showing up early for.

That is the shift worth noticing. Downtown Burbank signed leases with ten new tenants in a single year, arriving alongside roughly 1,000 new housing units and 300 hotel rooms in the district. The festivals residents already had on their calendars now sit inside a denser, more walkable eight-block grid than they did last summer. The itinerary changed even if the marquee events did not.

### The First Week Belongs to the Screen

The Burbank International Film Festival runs August 2 through 8, with screenings clustered at AMC 16 on East Palm Avenue. It is the anchor event of the month for a reason. Programming spans 120-plus screenings with filmmaker Q&As and red-carpet events, and the whole thing sits within a five-minute walk of the newest food openings in the district.

That last part is the part that has changed. If you have been to the festival before, you know the drill: catch a matinee, wander out for something quick, come back for the evening block. The "something quick" list is different in 2026.

- Tigawok, one of the openings Downtown Burbank announced last year, is now operating.

- Chubby Dumpling and Jam Jam Tea Studio opened in the same wave.

- Flow Wine & Coffee, from Burbank residents Vincent Tempongko and Ariel Nicastro, was built around LaMill coffee by day and hard-to-find wines by night, which is exactly the pacing a film festival demands.

- Nick the Greek opened at 3011 N. Hollywood Way earlier this year, roughly ten minutes from the AMC by car and a reasonable pre-screening detour if you are coming from the airport side of town.

None of that was here in the same configuration two summers ago. The film festival used to send people back to their cars between screenings. It no longer has to.

### A Week Later, Everything Turns Into a Comedy Room

The Burbank Comedy Festival runs August 15 through 22, hosted by Flappers Comedy Club, with celebrity headliners and more than 300 performers cycling through venues over eight days.

If you live here, the useful thing to understand is the density. Flappers sits inside the same Downtown grid as the new tenants above, which means the pre-show and post-show windows are genuinely walkable for the first time in a while. Lab Lagree opened as part of the same leasing wave for anyone who wants to earn the seat. Longer term, the district has also announced Scum & Villainy: Rendezvous Cantina, a fandom-focused bar and restaurant planned for a 5,300-square-foot space at 346 North First Street with an opening targeted for later in 2026. It will not be open in time for this year's comedy festival, but it is worth knowing where it is going, because that stretch of First Street is about to become a different block.

A few other names appear on the city's economic development list as anticipated but not yet open: Reve Café, Supreme Crab, Mom's Bakery, and WhataPeach. Addresses on an official list are not the same as confirmed opening dates, so treat them as previews rather than plans.

### The Nights That Live Outside Downtown

Not everything in August happens on San Fernando Boulevard. A quick reference for the weeks the festivals leave gaps:

| Date | Event | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fri, Jul 31 | Candlelight: Tribute to Fleetwood Mac / Michael Jackson | LA Equestrian Center, 480 W. Riverside Dr. |
| Sat, Aug 1 | Candlelight: Tribute to Maná | LA Equestrian Center |
| Sat, Aug 8 | Starlight Bowl: The Fab Four | 1249 Lockheed View Dr. |
| Fri, Aug 28 | Heidi Duckler Dance presents ¡Ordena! | Playclothes area, 3100 Magnolia Blvd. |
| Aug 29–30 | Free Shakespeare in the Park for Families | Lincoln Park at Buena Vista Library |
| Through Sep 7 | Richard Orlinski outdoor sculpture exhibition | Downtown Burbank |

A few notes on the ones worth planning around.

Starlight Bowl operates as an open-air hillside amphitheater above Lockheed View Drive. Parking runs $15, cash only, and tickets sit in the $18 to $25 range depending on how you pay. The Fab Four on August 8 is the tribute-band draw, but the season is built around the same premise every summer: a hillside seat, a picnic, and a short drive home.

Heidi Duckler Dance's ¡Ordena! is the sleeper pick of the month. It is an interactive food-truck performance staged during Magnolia Park Food Truck Fridays on August 28, with dancers and live jazz musicians fulfilling audience "orders" from a menu of dishes. The truck parks near Playclothes at 3100 Magnolia Boulevard, which is the same stretch of Magnolia Park that anchors much of the city's independent retail. If you have not been to a Food Truck Friday in a while, this is a reason to go back.

Shakespeare in the Park for Families, presented by The Actors' Gang, runs the last weekend of August at Lincoln Park behind the Buena Vista Library. Free, midday, family-oriented, and one of the quieter ways to close out the month.

Richard Orlinski's outdoor sculpture exhibition stays up in Downtown Burbank through September 7. It is worth building a walk around, especially before a screening or a comedy set, because the pieces are scaled for the sidewalks they sit on and reward the detour.

### What the Density Actually Changes

Downtown Burbank has more than 400 shops, restaurants, and services inside a walkable mixed-use district. Ten new tenants signed in a single year is not a facelift. It is a small but real change in what a Saturday can look like.

The practical version of that observation: a resident planning an August weekend used to build the day around the venue. You picked Starlight Bowl and worked backwards from Lockheed View. You picked the film festival and accepted that dinner would be whatever you could get near Palm Avenue.

This summer, the reverse also works. You can start with dinner at Flow Wine & Coffee or Tigawok, decide whether you want a screening or a comedy set based on what time you finish, and walk to the venue. That is a different way to live in a neighborhood, and it is the reason the August calendar reads differently than it did in 2024.

A few pragmatic reminders. New restaurants often see long waits and shifting hours during their first weeks, so keep a backup saved on your phone. Anticipated openings on the city's economic development list can slip, and construction, permits, and staffing all decide the actual date. Confirm hours before you make a special trip.

### A Note on the Rest of the Fall

The month closes with the Burbank Farmers Market, now in its 40th year and one of the oldest in Southern California, still running weekly. AfroAnimation Summit and the district's larger animation-industry events return in November, and the Downtown Burbank Holiday Market with 180-plus artisan vendors is already scheduled for December 12 through 13. If August is the month that rewards planning, September and October are the months that reward habit. The venues that felt new this summer will feel familiar by then, which is the point.

### Let's Connect

If you have been in Burbank long enough to remember when the block between the AMC and Flappers had three empty storefronts, you already know why this August feels different. If you are thinking about what your next chapter in the neighborhood looks like, whether that is a move up, a move down the hill, or a first purchase near Magnolia Park, Stacey Leahy is happy to walk the same blocks with you.
